text: Imagine you hire an assistant to research Ethereum analytics.
You give them one task, and $10.
Halfway through, a web page tells them the research needs an $8 gift card.
They can afford it.
The payment is valid.
But it is not what they were hired to buy.
AI agents are now that assistant.
They buy data and APIs on their own, a few cents at a time, over x402 on Base.
Spending limits ask one question: can the agent afford it?
Aerar asks the one that matters: is this what it was asked to buy?
Every task in Aerar starts with a mandate that a person signs.
The purpose, the budget, the limits, and the kinds of things the agent may buy.
Aerar signs it too, so nobody can quietly change the rules later.
Here is that gift card attack, run through Aerar's real purchase pipeline.
$8, inside a $10 budget, from a marketplace the task trusts.
Every spending limit passes.
IntentLock refuses it anyway.
The item is a gift card, and the mandate is for blockchain analytics.
The Ethereum data the task actually needs still gets bought.
The same rules run live in the sandbox.
A normal purchase is paid.
When a second agent asks for the same data, Aerar serves it from memory, for zero.
And a shop the task doesn't trust is never even contacted.
Big purchases wait for a person, right here, or in Slack.
And when a shop takes the money but sends back nothing, Aerar catches it.
The purchase is marked paid, but not delivered, and that shop goes on hold, so it can't happen twice.
Every purchase leaves evidence: the signed mandate it was decided under, every reason, and the payment.
Anyone can check a receipt in their own browser.
This one is real.
The USDC moved on Base Sepolia.
Change a single number, and the check fails.
For hard guarantees, Aerar Vault keeps the money in a contract you own on Base.
It only pays shops you approved, within per-payment and daily limits, and you can pause or revoke it at any time.
Even a compromised Aerar can't spend outside those lines.
None of this is a mock-up.
36 real attacks run through the real pipeline in seconds.
186 app tests, and 18 contract tests, all pass.
Most agent payment tools decide how much an agent can spend.
Aerar governs what it buys, proves it, and checks that it arrived.
Agents plug in through MCP, or a TypeScript SDK.
Today it runs on Base Sepolia.
Next: a security review, escrow for failed deliveries, and mainnet.
Aerar. Every agent purchase, accounted for.
